subject: history
title: Stalin's Terror and Industrialisation
welcome_lead: Five-Year Plans, gulags and show trials remake the Soviet Union.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on Stalin's industrialisation, collectivisation and Great Terror.
final_note: You have travelled from Magnitogorsk to the Lubyanka.

concepts.def: Centrally planned industrial targets; the First Plan ran 1928-32 prioritising heavy industry.
Forced merger of peasant farms into kolkhozes from 1929, eliminating kulaks as a class.
Famine of 1932-33 in Ukraine and Kazakhstan killing an estimated 5-7 million amid grain seizures.
1935 campaign celebrating shock-workers exceeding output targets, named after miner Alexei Stakhanov.
Purges of 1936-38 including show trials and mass executions; about 750,000 shot under NKVD Order 00447.
Network of labour camps administered by the NKVD; population peaked at about 2.5 million in the early 1950s.

walkthroughs.body_html: The 1927 grain procurement crisis convinced Stalin that NEP could not finance rapid industrialisation. Collectivisation provided cheap grain for export, urban food supply and political control over the peasantry. Dekulakisation deported about 1.8 million in 1930-31. Despite resistance, 93 per cent of households were collectivised by 1937, though productivity stagnated and livestock numbers collapsed.

First Five-Year Plan (1928-32) prioritised steel, coal and machinery. Iconic projects included Dneprostroi dam, Magnitogorsk steel works and Moscow Metro. Pig iron rose from 3.3 to 6.2 million tonnes; consumer goods stagnated. The Second Plan (1933-37) emphasised infrastructure; the Third (1938-41) prioritised armaments. The USSR became an industrial power, decisive for surviving Nazi invasion.

Kirov's assassination on 1 December 1934 triggered escalating purges. Three Moscow show trials (1936, 1937, 1938) eliminated Old Bolsheviks. NKVD Order 00447 of July 1937 set regional execution quotas. Robert Conquest's totalitarian model emphasises Stalin's agency; revisionists like J. Arch Getty stress chaotic central-local dynamics. Approximately 750,000 were shot and 1.5 million sentenced to camps in 1937-38.

mcqs.q: When did the First Five-Year Plan begin?

options: The 1932-33 famine in Ukraine
The 1934 purge of Leningrad
The 1937 show trial of Bukharin
The 1929 grain crisis

mcqs.q: Why did Stalin launch the Great Terror?
options: A combination of genuine paranoia, removal of political rivals, consolidation of personal power, and the dynamics of a self-reinforcing security apparatus.
The Five Year Plans were Lenin's last great achievement.
The Terror was a response to a planned coup by Trotsky.
Stalin was simply mentally ill and killed people at random.

mcqs.q: How successful were Stalin's Five Year Plans?
options: The Terror was a response to a planned coup by Trotsky.
The Five Year Plans were Lenin's last great achievement.
The Five Year Plans turned the USSR into the most prosperous country in the world.
Heavy industry and steel output grew dramatically; consumer goods, quality and worker conditions lagged badly; statistics were inflated, but the USSR became an industrial power.

mcqs.q: Who were the main victims of the Great Terror?
options: Old Bolsheviks, the military officer corps, ethnic minorities, kulaks, ordinary citizens denounced by neighbours, and eventually the NKVD itself — millions arrested or shot, 1936-38.
Stalin only purged Jews and Ukrainians.
The Terror was a response to a planned coup by Trotsky.
Stalin only purged senior Communist Party rivals.
